content: The pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) is designed to protect against pneumococcal disease, which is caused by pneumococcal bacteria. These bacteria are responsible for a variety of illnesses, including pneumonia, which is an infection of the lungs. Pneumococcal bacteria are among the most common causes of pneumonia. In addition to pneumonia, these bacteria can lead to ear infections, sinus infections, meningitis (an infection of the protective tissues surrounding the brain and spinal cord), and bacteremia (a bloodstream infection). While anyone can contract pneumococcal disease, certain groups are at higher risk. These include children under the age of 2, individuals with specific medical conditions, adults aged 65 or older, and cigarette smokers. Although most pneumococcal infections are mild, some can result in severe complications, such as brain damage or hearing loss. Serious forms of pneumococcal disease, such as meningitis, bacteremia, and pneumonia, can be life-threatening. The PPSV23 vaccine provides protection against 23 different types of pneumococcal bacteria. It is recommended for all adults aged 65 years or older, as well as for individuals aged 2 years or older who have certain medical conditions that increase their risk of pneumococcal disease. Most people require only one dose of PPSV23. However, a second dose of PPSV23, along with another pneumococcal vaccine called PCV13, may be recommended for individuals in high-risk groups. Your healthcare provider can offer more specific guidance. Adults aged 65 or older should receive a dose of PPSV23 even if they were vaccinated with it before turning 65. Before receiving the PPSV23 vaccine, inform your healthcare provider if you have ever had an allergic reaction to a previous dose of PPSV23 or if you have any severe, life-threatening allergies. In some cases, your provider may decide to delay vaccination until a later time. Individuals with minor illnesses, such as a cold, can still be vaccinated. However, those who are moderately or severely ill should typically wait until they recover before receiving PPSV23. Your healthcare provider can provide additional information. After receiving the PPSV23 vaccine, some individuals may experience redness or pain at the injection site, fatigue, fever, or muscle aches. Fainting can occasionally occur after medical procedures, including vaccinations. If you feel dizzy, experience changes in vision, or notice ringing in your ears, inform your provider immediately. As with any medication, there is an extremely small chance of a severe allergic reaction, serious injury, or death following vaccination. If a severe allergic reaction occurs after leaving the clinic, seek emergency medical attention immediately. Signs of a severe allergic reaction include hives, swelling of the face and throat, difficulty breathing, a rapid heartbeat, dizziness, or weakness. Call 9-1-1 and go to the nearest hospital. For other concerning symptoms, contact your healthcare provider. Adverse reactions should be reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). Your healthcare provider can file this report, or you can do so yourself by visiting the VAERS website or calling 1-800-822-7967. Please note that VAERS is only for reporting reactions and does not provide medical advice. For additional information about the PPSV23 vaccine, consult your healthcare provider, contact your local or state health department, or reach out to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). You can call 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visit the CDC's vaccine website. Vaccine information statements are also available in Spanish and many other languages at www.immunize.org/vis.
